scenes.title: Pause and try: improve a description

items.text: What does it do? When should the model use it? What does it return?

items.q: Does the model run the tool itself?
items.a: No. The model only **requests** a call: it returns a `tool_use` block with a name and input. **Your code** runs the function and sends the output back as a `tool_result` with the same id.
items.trap: Saying "Claude executes my function". It never touches your code; you decide whether and how to run it.

items.q: What makes a good tool definition?
items.a: A clear verb **name**, a **description** that says what it does, when to use it and what it returns, and a tight **schema** (enums, required fields, `strict: true`).
items.trap: Focusing only on the schema. The description is what the model reads to choose the tool.

captions.text: Welcome to Module 5.
In Module 4 you built an agent loop with two small tools.
Now we go deeper into the tools themselves.
By the end of this module, you'll build a personal productivity agent that manages
real tasks and notes, checks every input, stops slow tools, and asks you before it
deletes anything.
In this lesson, you'll learn what tool calling is, and why it exists.
You'll follow one tool call from the request to the result.
You'll read every part of a tool definition.
And you'll write tool descriptions that a model uses correctly.
Let's start with what a tool is, using an everyday picture.
Imagine you hire an assistant.
They're smart, but they can't reach into your calendar or your files directly.
So you lend them a phone with a few apps.
Each app has a clear label, saying what it does, and a form to fill in.
The model is the assistant.
It decides which app to open, and what to type in the form.
A tool is one app: a name, a description of what it does, and a form for its inputs.
And your code is the phone.
It's the part that actually runs the app, and shows the result.
So why does tool calling exist?
Because a language model on its own can only write text.
It can't read your to-do list, save a note, or check today's date.
Tools let it ask your code to do those things, safely, through doors you choose.
Now how does it work?
Let's follow one tool call, step by step.
Step one.
Your code sends a request with two things: the user's message, and the list of tools
the model may use.
Step two.
The model decides a tool would help.
Instead of a final answer, it replies with a tool use block: the tool's name, the
input it wants, and an ID.
The stop reason is tool use.
Step three.
Your code runs the real function with that input.
This is important: the model never runs anything itself.
It only asks.
Step four.
Your code sends the output back as a tool result, with the same ID, in the next
request.
Then the model continues, and either asks for another tool, or answers.
Let's see that in real code.
The code is on the left, and what it printed is on the right.
A tool definition is a Python dictionary.
First, a name, and a description written for the model.
The description is how the model decides when to use this tool.
Next, the input schema.
It's a JSON Schema: a standard way to describe data.
Here the form has three fields: a title, a due date that can be empty, and a
priority that must be low, normal or high.
And strict, true.
With strict mode, the API guarantees that the input the model sends matches this
schema: the right fields, and the right types.
Then we pass the tool in the tools list, next to the messages.
The first output line is the offline notice: as in every module, a scripted fake
plays the model, so no key is needed.
The stop reason is tool use.
The model didn't answer.
It's asking our code to run a tool.
And here's the tool use block: the name, add task, and the input, title pay rent, no
due date, priority high.
Notice that nothing has been added yet.
Our code would run the function next.
We'll do that in lesson two.
Let's put every part in one table.
The name: short, unique, and usually a verb, like add task.
The description: when to use the tool, and what it returns.
This is the model's only guide, so it's the most important part.
The input schema: the fields, their types, and the allowed values.
And strict: when it's true, the inputs always match the schema.
Now, where do developers go wrong?
Mostly in the description.
A name like task, and a description like task tool, tells the model almost nothing.
Does it add a task?
Delete one?
List them?
A clear description says three things.
What the tool does: adds a task and returns its number.
When to use it: when the user asks to remember or plan something.
And any rules: the due date must be today or later.
Write it as if for a new colleague who has never seen your app.
Pause the video and try it.
Here's a tool called notes, with the description: notes.
Rewrite the name and the description.
Ask yourself: what does it do, when should the model use it, and what does it
return?
One good answer: name it search notes.
Description: searches the user's notes for words in the title or text, and returns
the matching notes.
Use it when the user asks about something they saved earlier.
Interview corner.
Here's a common question.
Does the model run the tool itself?
A good answer: no.
The model only requests a call, by returning a tool use block with a name and an
input.
Your code runs the function, and sends the output back as a tool result with the
same ID.
The trap is saying the model executes your function.
It never touches your code.
You decide whether to run it.
And a follow-up: what makes a good tool definition?
A clear verb for the name, a description that says what the tool does, when to use
it, and what it returns, and a tight schema, with enums, required fields, and strict
mode.
The trap: focusing only on the schema.
The description is what the model reads to choose the tool.
Quick check.
The stop reason is tool use.
What should your code do?
Run the requested tool, and send the output back as a tool result with the same ID.
Let's recap.
Tools let a model ask your code to act in the world.
The model requests, your code runs the function, and the result goes back with the
same ID.
A definition has a name, a description, an input schema, and strict mode.
And the description is the model's guide: what it does, when to use it, what it
returns, and the rules.
Next lesson: many tools in one place.
You'll build a tool registry, generate schemas from Pydantic, and handle several
tool calls in a single turn.
